procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated July 7, 1953, of the Assam High Court in Civil Rules Nos. 147 and 148 of 1952.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Assam High Court reviewed the decision of the Deputy Commissioner, Sibsagar, via Civil Rules Nos. 147 and 148 of 1952, which were applications under Article 226 (likely for writs). The High Court refused to issue the writs, being satisfied that there was no failure of justice.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed the High Court's judgment to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court's discretion, finding no reason to believe that the justice of the case required such interference. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether a claim for extra wages for work done beyond a basic task amounts to a claim arising out of the payment of less than the minimum rates of wages under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.

facts: The government issued a notification increasing the minimum basic wages for tea plantation labourers.
Prior to this, labourers were paid a basic wage for a specific workload (e.g., 16 seers of tea leaves for men) and received extra pay for any leaves plucked beyond that amount.
After the notification, the employers paid the new, higher minimum basic wage but refused to pay extra wages unless the labourers plucked a much larger quantity of leaves (e.g., 24 seers for men).
The labourers filed a claim under Section 20 of the Minimum Wages Act, arguing they were entitled to extra wages for work done beyond the original, lower workload.
law: The employers (appellants) argued that the claim was for "extra wages" over and above the minimum wage, not a claim "arising out of the payment of less than the minimum rates of wages." Therefore, they contended the authority under Section 20 of the Act had no jurisdiction to hear the case.

The labourers (respondents) argued that the minimum basic wage was correlated to the existing, lower workload. They contended that the employers' refusal to pay for extra work beyond that original task was "tantamount to non-payment of the minimum basic wages" and thus fell within the jurisdiction of the Act.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged the two competing arguments regarding jurisdiction.
It noted the employers' position that since the new basic wage was being paid, the dispute was only about extra wages and outside the scope of the Act.
It also noted the labourers' counter-argument that the failure to pay for work beyond the established basic task effectively constituted a payment of less than the minimum wage.
However, the Court observed that the High Court had already fully adjudicated the main dispute between the parties.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court explicitly declined to decide the question of jurisdiction. It reasoned that since the case had been pending for a long time (since 1952) and the High Court had already ruled on the substance of the dispute, no useful purpose would be served by interfering on a jurisdictional point at such a late stage. By refusing to overturn the lower court's decision on this ground, the Court effectively rejected the employers' challenge for the purposes of this specific case.

issue.issue_text: Whether a writ of certiorari can be refused by the High Court if it is satisfied that there was no failure of justice.

facts: The case reached the Supreme Court as an appeal against a judgment of the High Court of Assam.
The High Court had dismissed an application under Article 226 of the Constitution, which sought a writ of certiorari against orders from a Deputy Commissioner.
law: The Supreme Court established that a writ of certiorari is not granted automatically or "as a matter of course."
The High Court has the power and is entitled to refuse to issue the writ if it is satisfied that there has been no failure of justice.
The Supreme Court will not interfere with the High Court's exercise of discretion in such matters unless it is satisfied that the "justice of the case requires" its interference.
application: The Supreme Court noted that in this specific case, both the Deputy Commissioner and the High Court had concurrently found in favor of the respondents on the merits of the dispute.
The Supreme Court agreed with these concurrent findings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since there was no failure of justice on the merits of the case, the High Court was correct in exercising its discretion to refuse the writ of certiorari. Consequently, the Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the discretionary orders of the High Court in an appeal unless the justice of the case requires such interference.

facts: The case reached the Supreme Court as an appeal against a High Court's judgment.
The High Court had exercised its discretionary power under Article 226 of the Constitution to refuse to issue a writ of certiorari.
The merits of the underlying dispute had been concurrently found in favor of the respondents by both the initial authority (the Deputy Commissioner) and the High Court.
law: A writ of certiorari is not granted as a matter of course; the High Court has the discretion to refuse the writ if it is satisfied there was no failure of justice.
The Supreme Court's standard for intervention in an appeal against such a discretionary order is whether the "justice of the case requires such interference."
application: The Supreme Court noted that it was not hearing a direct appeal from the initial order but was reviewing the High Court's discretionary refusal to intervene.
The Court considered the merits of the case and the fact that two lower forums (the Deputy Commissioner and the High Court) had already ruled in favor of the respondents.
Based on these concurrent findings on the merits, the Supreme Court was "not satisfied that the justice of the case requires it" to interfere with the High Court's decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it would not interfere with the High Court's discretionary order. It established and applied the principle that it will only intervene in such cases if it is satisfied that the justice of the case requires it. Since the merits had been consistently decided in favor of the respondents by the lower forums, the Court found no such requirement for justice and declined to interfere, dismissing the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a claim for extra wages for work done beyond a basic task amounts to a claim arising out of the payment of less than the minimum rates of wages under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
appellant_arguments: The applications filed by the labourers were not maintainable under section 20 of the Minimum Wages Act.
The minimum basic wages fixed by the government were not correlated to the existing work-load or task.
The provision to continue the existing work-load was only intended to prevent employers from increasing the task to make up for the wage increase, not to link the basic wage to a specific output.
respondent_arguments: The claim is maintainable under section 20 of the Act because not paying for work beyond the basic task amounts to a payment of less than the minimum wage.
The government's notification intended to increase the basic wages for the same basic work-load that existed previously (16 seers for males, 12 seers for females).
Labourers are entitled to extra payment for green leaves plucked in excess of the basic task.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a writ of certiorari can be refused by the High Court if it is satisfied that there was no failure of justice.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should have issued the writ to quash the order of the Deputy Commissioner due to legal errors.
respondent_arguments: The High Court has the discretion to refuse a writ of certiorari, as it is not granted 'as a matter of course'.
The writ can be refused if the court is satisfied that, on the merits of the case, there has been no failure of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the discretionary orders of the High Court in an appeal unless the justice of the case requires such interference.
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court should interfere because the High Court wrongly exercised its discretion by refusing to issue the writ.
The justice of the case requires interference to correct the errors of the lower authorities.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with the High Court's discretionary order, especially when there are concurrent findings of fact in the respondent's favour.
Interference is not warranted as the justice of the case does not require it.

cases.citation: Hailsham Edition, Vol. 9, para. 1480 and 1481, pp. 877-878
cases.principle: Proceedings by way of certiorari are 'not of Course', and a High Court has the power to refuse the writ if it is satisfied that there was no failure of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A writ of certiorari is not granted as a matter of course. A High Court has the discretion to refuse the writ if it is satisfied that there has been no failure of justice. In an appeal from such a decision, the Supreme Court will not interfere with the High Court's exercise of discretion unless the justice of the case requires it.
obiter: Whether a claim for extra wages for work performed beyond a basic task, where the minimum wage for that basic task has already been paid, constitutes a 'claim arising out of the payment of less than the minimum rates of wages' within the meaning of section 20(2) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The sole intention of the Government in issuing the notification was to increase the basic wages of as. 8/- and as. 6/- to as. 12/- and as. 11/- respectively while maintaining the same basic work-load or task assigned to the male and female labourers. The acceptance of the appellant's contention would mean that no advantage whatever was sought to be conferred by the Government on the labourers, an intention which can scarcely be attributed to the Government. Therefore, the labourers are entitled to be paid the new basic wages for the pre-existing workload (16 seers for males, 12 seers for females) and are entitled to extra wages for every seer of green leaves plucked over and above those quantities.
legal_tests_applied: A writ of certiorari is 'not of Course' and a High Court has the power to refuse the writ if it is satisfied that there was no failure of justice.
The Supreme Court can refuse to interfere with a High Court's discretionary order in an appeal under Article 226 unless it is satisfied that the justice of the case requires such interference.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the notification fixed only a 'minimum time rate' irrespective of output was rejected as 'obviously unsound' because the notification itself stated that 'the existing tasks and hours of work shall continue until further orders.' The court reasoned that if the wages were fixed irrespective of the task, there would have been no need to include this provision.

The court declined to interfere with the High Court's discretionary refusal to issue a writ of certiorari, affirming that the High Court had the power to do so because it was satisfied there was no failure of justice.

The court refused to exercise its own discretion to interfere with the High Court's order because it was not satisfied that the justice of the case required it, especially given the concurrent findings of fact in favour of the respondents by both the Deputy Commissioner and the High Court.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's interpretation that the government notification correlated the new, higher basic wages to the existing workload. The court found that the evidence and the text of the notification supported the conclusion that the basic wages were for a specific task (16 seers for males, 12 for females) and any work beyond that required extra payment.
The court affirmed the High Court's discretionary power to refuse a writ of certiorari when it determines there has been no failure of justice on the merits of the case.
The court agreed that it should not interfere with the High Court's order, noting the concurrent findings of fact in the respondent's favour by two lower forums.
policy_considerations: The court adopted a purposive interpretation of the government notification, reasoning that its intent must have been to confer a real benefit on the labourers, which would not have happened under the appellant's interpretation.

The court considered judicial finality and efficiency, stating that since the matters had been pending for over four years and the High Court had already adjudicated the main disputes, 'no useful purpose will be served by our interfering at this stage.'
